title: New Tax Credit Program Sparks Questions Over Special Education Services
summary: As the mother of a son with autism, Angie Pannuti knows what it’s like to negotiate with a school district for special education services. “Every meeting is the same,” she said, describing conferences with officials in eastern Kentucky’s Greenup County schools. “You will hear, ‘That is not how we do it.’ “ She called her […]
content: As the mother of a son with autism, Angie Pannuti knows what it’s like to negotiate with a school district for special education services. “Every meeting is the same,” she said, describing conferences with officials in eastern Kentucky’s Greenup County schools. “You will hear, ‘That is not how we do it.’ “ She called her oldest son’s preschool years “baptism by fire” because of the frequency with which she left those discussions without answers. Now, at 8, her son loves school and spends most of his time in a regular classroom. But Pannuti’s experience inspired her to launch Special Education Lifeline , a nonprofit, to support other parents going through similar struggles. When she heard about the new Federal Scholarship Tax Credit, which will direct taxpayer donations toward students, she jumped at the chance to become a scholarship granting organization serving kids in Kentucky’s public schools. “If I can legally use it to help families that are already marginalized, yeah, absolutely,” she said. Angie Pannuti with sons Matthew, left and Michael, and husband Thomas. She has formed a scholarship granting organization to support students with disabilities in public schools under the new Federal Scholarship Tax Credit program. (Courtesy of Angie Pannuti) But with a little more than a month until the program launches, she’s among those still awaiting further details from the Treasury Department on what the scholarships can pay for. The public can comment on proposed rules for the new program until Dec. 1 and dial into a Dec. 15 public hearing . The IRS said it will use that feedback to craft guidance on eligible expenses. When five Democratic governors asked for specifics in October, Kevin Salinger, acting chief counsel of the IRS, essentially said “stay tuned.” Officials plan a broad interpretation of the items and services parents can buy, but that doesn’t address how the scholarships might work for students who receive special education services in public schools. Related In Long Awaited Rules for Tax Credit Scholarships, Feds Stress Neediest Students In fact, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, who has not opted into the program, asked the Treasury Department about this issue in an Oct. 16 letter. He wanted to know “how special-needs services should be treated, given that services in a student’s individualized education program must be provided at no cost to families under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act.” But Salinger didn’t have much to offer. “The Treasury Department and the Internal Revenue Service cannot provide guidance on this question as it falls outside of the scope of tax law,” he wrote . He pointed Moore to the legislation, which borrows language from Coverdell education savings accounts, part of the existing tax code . That program allows parents to create tax-advantaged accounts for education expenses, including “special needs services in the case of a special needs beneficiary.” Those services, such as therapies and additional technology, would be supplemental to what a child receives in school. Jim Blew, an advisor to the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit Coalition, a nonprofit focusing on implementation, said there shouldn’t be any cause for confusion. Scholarships can’t pay for the “expenses that the taxpayers are already obliged to cover” under a student’s individualized education program and the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, he said. But advocates for students with disabilities say parents and school districts are bound to have questions. “This vagueness creates the misleading impression that scholarship-funded private options or external service providers may offer standard special education services and can be reimbursed to provide them,” the Council of Parent Attorneys and Advocates, or COPAA, wrote in an explainer about the new program. They want the IRS to clarify that the scholarships “may only reimburse supplemental services that go beyond” what’s included in a student’s IEP or 504 plan under the Rehabilitation Act. ‘As successful as they should be’ COPAA is among the organizations that encouraged governors not to opt into the program, warning that if students with disabilities use a scholarship to attend a private school, they’ll give up the civil rights protections guaranteed under IDEA. With states and school districts hoping to maximize this program for kids in public school, advocates are closely watching how the scholarships, funded by taxpayer donations, could complement mandated services in schools. A student’s IEP should include the services a student needs “to not just thrive, to be literally as successful as they should be,” said Jacqueline Rodriguez, CEO of the National Center for Learning Disabilities. But federal, state and local funds fall short, and parents often pay out of pocket for private therapists, evaluations and other services. Related Private Equity Is Cashing in on Autism Therapy. Children Are Paying the Price Marguerite Roza , director of Edunomics, a Georgetown University think tank, says the new program could create a legal gray area. “The minute the school says a student with disabilities needs a service, then the school must provide it for free,” she said. “That doesn’t keep kids with disabilities from seeking tutoring or summer programs, but does make it hard for the district to recommend or facilitate that. My guess is that we’ll see some lawsuits on this issue.” To Rodriguez, the uncertainty suggests that an agency without education expertise shouldn’t be making the rules. State officials will have to make “impactful significant decisions about how to interpret this program,” she said. Jessica Saum, a special education coordinator in Arkansas’ Cabot school district, north of Little Rock, said parents frequently ask for advice about external providers, but the district doesn’t make recommendations. “I don’t want to put my name on it if they have a bad experience,” she said. The federal program, she said, leaves her with questions. If a student receives a scholarship for a supplemental program for a year, “is the public school going to be required or expected to continue providing that service?” Jessica Saum, left, pictured with student Lilly Kittinger, is a special education coordinator in Arkansas’ Cabot Public Schools. (Courtesy of Jessica Saum) In Sioux Falls, South Dakota, a new SGO recently launched to “make sure that we’re prepared to accept the dollars,” said Superintendent Jamie Nold. But he’s still in the dark about those additional services for students in special education. He suspects that students with IEPs will use the funds for tutoring related to their disability. That’s currently what a lot of families pay for on their own, he said. Dan Gordon, a senior legal and policy advisor for EducationCounsel, a law and advocacy firm, offered another example: A student’s IEP might call for two sessions a week with an occupational therapist, but maybe the family uses a scholarship for a third. He called the lack of clarity “100% something the field needs guidance on.” “It’s definitely something that has come up a lot in our conversations with both national organizations and state and local education leaders,” he said. “There’s a mix of rights, opportunities and tensions at play here.” ‘Realities families experience’ The topic came up during a Connecticut special education conference in October, with experts saying SGOs will have to be careful not to charge families for services their children are entitled to under IDEA. Whatever guidance the Treasury Department issues, one parent among the 25,000 individuals and groups who have already submitted comments asked officials to consider the hurdles that children with disabilities already face. “My request is that the regulations implementing it reflect the realities families experience,” wrote Mindi R. from Indiana , whose child has autism and behavioral health needs. “Parents of children with disabilities already spend enormous amounts of time navigating complicated systems. Educational scholarships should make accessing appropriate services easier, not introduce another system of confusing eligibility requirements, financial barriers and unclear protections.” Related New Tax Credit Program Sparks Questions Over Special Education Services Frustration with special education services in public schools is one reason why state private school choice programs are so popular, said Blew, with the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit Coalition. A recent report on Arkansas’ Education Freedom Accounts, for example, shows that more than 16% of students enrolled have disabilities, which is higher than the share of K-12 students with disabilities statewide. In Texas, data shows more than a quarter of students enrolled in that state’s private school choice program have a disability. But Kentucky doesn’t have an ESA program. And in Pennuti’s region of the state, there are very few private schools and “zero schools focused on children with exceptionalities,” she said. That’s why she hopes public school students will be able to benefit from the federal program. “Everybody talks about school choice. We don’t have school choice.”

title: Some 2M Children Have Lost SNAP Benefits — And Now Millions More Are at Risk
summary: Staff at Madrona Elementary School in Seattle spent last Friday stocking a brand new food pantry opened on-site to meet the community’s growing demand for help after drastic cuts to federal aid programs. Principal Regina Carter said the types of families seeking food assistance have widened dramatically this year as local residents face high gas, […]
content: Staff at Madrona Elementary School in Seattle spent last Friday stocking a brand new food pantry opened on-site to meet the community’s growing demand for help after drastic cuts to federal aid programs. Principal Regina Carter said the types of families seeking food assistance have widened dramatically this year as local residents face high gas, grocery and utility costs — along with skyrocketing rent. “We’ve been really surprised by how many families are asking for support,” Carter said. “It’s not just our students who are considered furthest away from educational justice or, (those experiencing homelessness). It’s families with two parents in the home who have fallen on hard times and just need a little bit of help.” Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter Last year’s Republican-led budget bill cut funding to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, and enacted tougher eligibility and expanded work requirements. The result was an estimated 5.5 million people pushed off the rolls, some 2 million of them children . Erin Hysom, senior child nutrition policy analyst, Food Research & Action Center. (Erin Hysom) And because SNAP eligibility automatically qualifies students for free meals at school, that means more kids are going hungry at home while also finding it harder to access food between classes. “What’s not always known or well understood is the interconnectedness between federal nutrition programs and children who receive SNAP,” said Erin Hysom, senior child nutrition policy analyst with the Food Research & Action Center. “They are automatically eligible to receive free school meals. So when you cut one side of the equation, you are jeopardizing the other.” A decrease in the number of kids on SNAP might also impact the Community Eligibility Provision, which, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture , allows the nation’s highest-poverty schools and districts to serve breakfast and lunch at no cost to all students — without requiring families to submit cumbersome applications. FRAC points out that CEP schools that no longer meet the threshold will lose their eligibility and others might chose to drop out because decreased SNAP participation means smaller federal reimbursement rates. Related North Carolina Child Hunger Leaders Discuss Looming SNAP Cuts That situation could soon worsen. Earlier this month, the USDA, which oversees SNAP, issued a proposed rule to eliminate what’s known as broad-based categorical eligibility. That allows states to identify a wider swath of families as being in need of federal food assistance if they also receive other types of public benefits. The department estimates the change could drop 6.3 million more people from SNAP, forcing the families of nearly 1.8 million children to now have to fill out the paperwork to receive free and reduced-priced meals at school. Hysom said individual applications for school-based food aid are complicated, costly for schools to process and needlessly embarrassing for applicants. “We hear from families that they might not want the school district to know that they’re struggling,” she said. “And when you think about a school district and you think about who works for a school system, those are our neighbors, our community members, the people we go to church with, the people we play sports with. If you’re a family that’s fallen on hard times, you might not want your child’s Sunday school teacher or baseball coach to know that.” Some 41 million people benefitted from the SNAP program in August 2025. That figure shrank to roughly 36 million a year later, according to government records, marking a 13.4% drop. Stewart Fried, a principal attorney at OFW Law in Washington, D.C., and an expert on SNAP, said new restrictions on categorical eligibility could bring the number of program beneficiaries down to 30 million. Fried said he is unsure what the blue wave in this month’s midterm elections might do for food security. “Trump rolled out his veto hat … the night of the election, and he’s right,” Fried said. “Democrats don’t have close to the number of votes in the Senate to override a presidential veto. So we’re stuck with existing legislation unless someone convinces him that the Republicans are going to get clobbered in 2028 unless he cooperates.” Gina Plata-Nino, director of SNAP policy and advocacy, Food Research & Action Center. (Food Research & Action Center) The federal government has also lessened its financial contribution to the program: States began, in October, paying 75% of SNAP’s administrative costs — up from 50% — and many will later assume other, massive expenditures tied to providing the benefits themselves. Gina Plata-Nino, FRAC’s director of SNAP policy and advocacy, said there is no single attack on food security in the United States. “It’s an agenda,” she said, one that impacts many groups of people. “These are children, working families, veterans, older adults, people with disabilities.” One place where the Democrats’ sweeping victory could make a difference is at the state level. Several incoming governors — including Aaron Ford in Nevada , Rob Sand in Iowa , Cindy Holscher in Kansas and Amy Acton in Ohio — have all pledged to either reinstate or work to establish universal free meals in school. During her campaign, Acton frequently recalled being without food as a child and the “couple on the north side of Youngstown who used to pull my brother and I up on their front porch, walking by on the way to Harding Elementary, and feed us breakfast because they knew we were hungry.” Amy Acton, the state’s former director of the Department of Health, speaks to supporters during a rally on April 28, 2026, in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Jon Cherry/Getty Images) Holscher noted that “nearly 1 in 5 Kansas kids faces food insecurity and school meals help students show up ready to learn.” Island Harvest, which aids families in Suffolk and Nassau counties on Long Island, has more than 350 network partners, including soup kitchens, food pantries and emergency feeding programs. It distributed roughly 22 million pounds of food during the last fiscal year. Gregory May, its director of government and community relations, said the federal bill’s impact on families has been profound. He said there are roughly 250,000 people living with food insecurity in his coverage area, adding that more than 17,000 Nassau and Suffolk county residents have lost SNAP benefits since January. “We’ve had more than 92,000 new visits to our network of member agencies in 2026,” he said, adding the largest jump in new monthly visits came in June when the figure skyrocketed by 14,000. Related Families Brace for Tighter SNAP Work Requirements This was unsurprising. The federal government recently amended the existing 20-hour-per-week work requirement for SNAP recipients, expanding the age range by 10 years to 64 and allowing for fewer exemptions. Not all families can meet the new rules: Those who can’t are only eligible for SNAP for three months in a three-year period. “The three-month clock started in March,” May said. “As those SNAP benefits wound down, we saw a jump in new visits.” Island Harvest, which has a $15 million operating budget, has received help from New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, he said, adding he’s “incredibly grateful” for the $1 million in added money. FRAC’s Hysom called on Congress to immediately delay the benefit costs shifts that will hit states next year and to fully repeal the SNAP cuts before children are harmed any further. “We know the devastation that it’s creating in households and communities, and this ripple effect between the child nutrition programs, school meals, summer meals, WIC (SNAP for Women, Infants, and Children) and the interconnectedness of all these programs,” she said. Youth services assistant Charlotte Watson-King (left) and Principal Regina Carter (right) in Madrona Elementary School’s new pantry. (Regina Carter) The pantry, which stocks a variety of non-perishable goods, was recently opened to meet school families’ growing need for food assistance. (Regina Carter) Carter’s school in Washington state serves 248 students. Some 32% receive free or reduced-price lunch, a key indicator of poverty. Nineteen of her students are currently experiencing homelessness. Carter said the pantry, built with the support of partner organizations, is located in a vacant office, and is filled with non-perishable foods, including rice, canned goods and applesauce. The principal, like other child advocates who spoke with The 74 the week before Thanksgiving, said hunger greatly impedes a child’s ability to learn. “If your tummy’s grumbling, you’re not going to be able to focus,” Carter said. “So that has a huge impact on our students.” Related Judges Rule Trump Can’t Completely Stop SNAP Aid The new food pantry is one of several ways her school works to keep kids fed: they supply breakfast and lunch and weekend satchels — “Friday bags” — full of food to help families through the weekend. They do the same for holidays and other breaks, distributing gift cards from a variety of sources as needed. “Madrona is such a beautiful community,” Carter said. “There are so many people who want to help.”

title: Opinion: Teaching Kids to Read Is Important. So Is Teaching Them to Communicate
summary: Abraham Lincoln had less than a year of formal schooling, an awkward manner and a high-pitched voice. He became one of America’s greatest communicators through study and practice, not innate ability. As a boy, he learned storytelling from his father and repeated preachers’ sermons for other children. As a young man, he joined a debating […]
content: Abraham Lincoln had less than a year of formal schooling , an awkward manner and a high-pitched voice . He became one of America’s greatest communicators through study and practice, not innate ability. As a boy, he learned storytelling from his father and repeated preachers’ sermons for other children . As a young man, he joined a debating society; as a lawyer, he honed his powers of persuasion. The Gettysburg Address, with its vision of the nation’s future, was the product of a lifetime of practice. So were Lincoln’s interpersonal skills: As Doris Kearns Goodwin chronicled in “ Team of Rivals,” he brought political opponents into his cabinet and held that fractious group together by listening, telling stories and persuading — often one conversation at a time. Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter Few children will become prolific orators, but every child needs oracy , which Merriam-Webster defines as “proficiency in oral expression and comprehension.” That means explaining an idea clearly, listening, asking good questions and responding thoughtfully to others’ ideas. Like reading and writing, these skills should be taught and measured deliberately in school, for all children, starting in preschool. In most schools, they are not. At the University of Chicago Behavioral Insights and Parenting Lab , which I co-lead, we develop and evaluate tools to help parents and teachers build children’s 21st century skills. Oracy is one of them, and it matters more and more in the age of artificial intelligence. That’s because while AI can produce, summarize and vet information in seconds, it cannot substitute for human communication: explain reasoning to a skeptical colleague, read the room, pitch a creative idea or build trust. Related Nebraska Head Starts Use Vests With ‘Talk Pedometers’ to Boost Early Literacy Employers rank communication among the top skills they want in the people they hire, and the labor market rewarded it well before ChatGPT. From 1980 to 2012, jobs demanding strong social skills (persuading, negotiating, coordinating with others and reading their reactions) grew by nearly 12 percentage points as a share of U.S. employment, while math-heavy jobs requiring few social skills shrank. Speaking also signals competence: In a University of Chicago study , employers and recruiters rated candidates more competent, intelligent and hirable when they heard a pitch than when they read it. Interactive talk is also how children learn and learn to get along. In England, a randomized trial of an educational approach called Dialogic Teaching, which trains teachers to ask open-ended questions and push students to explain and build on one another’s answers, found that after 20 weeks, 9- and 10-year-olds in 72 primary schools were about two months ahead of peers on standardized tests in English and science, and one month ahead in math. In a review of 104 studies , young children’s stronger language skills were correlated with higher capabilities of understanding what others think and believe — a foundation for cooperation. Yet students practice these skills mainly in speech and debate , an extracurricular activity concentrated in private and higher-income public schools. In a random sample in New York City , 82% of independent secondary schools offered debate, versus 24% of public schools. That is a missed opportunity: Children who joined the Boston Debate League, a nonprofit serving mostly low-income public school students, were found to have gained about two-thirds of a typical ninth grade year’s learning in English and were more likely to graduate and enroll in college than non-participants. American early education focuses on teaching letters, their sounds and sight words because they are easy to teach and test. The Common Core and Head Start’s learning framework both include communication goals, but only 23 states’ science-of-reading laws mention oral language and writing. Head Start classrooms average 2.1 out of 7 on a standard measure of how teachers extend children’s thinking and talk. In Chicago-area pre-K and kindergarten classrooms my team observed , most teacher questions had one right answer, and most educators said they had never been trained to foster children’s language skills. Parents may need even more support. By 18 months , long before preschool, toddlers from lower-income families already lag in vocabulary. Conversations beyond the here and now — talk about the past and the future, how things work and make-believe — build language most. Yet in one study, such talk made up less than 10% of what parents said to 3½-year-olds. Related In Babies’ Brains, White Matter Is Crucial — and Conversational Turns Make It Grow Evidence on how to teach oracy is thin. A review of 33 trials of language- and literacy-focused training for preschool teachers found that children gained mainly in recognizing letters and their sounds; none of them captured whether children could explain an idea or hold a conversation. Similarly, a review of 25 randomized trials of parent coaching found the adults’ language changed far more than the children’s. The few programs targeting oracy, like Dialogic Teaching, rely on days of teacher training and ongoing mentoring, which are hard and expensive to scale. My team is testing a lower-cost approach. Our program, Chat2Learn , texts parents an illustrated, age-appropriate conversation starter several times a week, such as “What are some things kids can do that grown-ups can’t do?” Parents can share their child’s response or ask for an additional prompt to receive a follow-up query, turning one question into a productive back-and-forth. The prompts take the guesswork out of what to say; with practice, parents can build effective conversation habits. Early results are encouraging. In an experiment with 63 Chicago families, parents who received prompts asked more open-ended questions and used longer, more varied sentences than those who did not. We are now conducting a randomized trial of the parent program and testing a classroom version that coordinates conversations at school and at home around what children are learning. England is building oracy into its national curriculum , and Australia and New Zealand already treat communication as a core early-learning skill. The United States should, too. States should include speaking and listening along with reading and math in early-learning standards and assessments. Teacher training should cover building oracy, and schools from pre-K up should give parents concrete tools, such as ready-made conversation starters, to engage families in their children’s learning. Finally, educators and parents need more evidence on what builds oracy. Children growing up alongside machines that write fluently will stand out if they can do what machines cannot: explain, listen and connect. Disclosure: The Overdeck Family Foundation provides financial support to the University of Chicago Behavioral Insights and Parenting Lab and The 74 .

title: Opinion: To New Blue State Governors: Be an Education Governor
summary: Democrats have a long tradition of expanding opportunity through public education, and with 75% of the nation’s school-aged children in states with Democratic governors as of January, the practical work of improving student learning deserves a more prominent place in our national agenda. For too many years, the big “blue” ideas in education have amounted […]
content: Democrats have a long tradition of expanding opportunity through public education, and with 75% of the nation’s school-aged children in states with Democratic governors as of January, the practical work of improving student learning deserves a more prominent place in our national agenda. For too many years, the big “blue” ideas in education have amounted to “more money” and “less accountability.” New Democratic governors have an opportunity to bring fresh energy to this work, building on progress already underway and combining investment with honest accountability and sustained support for educators. There are useful lessons across the country. While student outcomes in many blue states drifted (or nosedived) downward, states such as Louisiana, Tennessee, Arkansas, and Mississippi quietly showed the way, with work rooted in strong evidence about how children learn and how school systems improve. On the 2024 National Assessment of Educational Progress, Louisiana’s fourth graders led the nation in reading growth for the second consecutive cycle and were among the few to exceed their pre-pandemic scores in both reading and math. Incoming governors should look closely at what is working, wherever it is happening, and adapt those lessons to their states. Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter Many new governors wisely make education policy a priority. It shapes their state’s economy, its civic life, and the opportunities open to every child who grows up there. We know far more than we used to about how to get results. Here is where to start. 1. Commit to goals for student learning, measure progress honestly, and report publicly Start by finding out whether your state’s tests are telling parents the truth. Compare your state’s proficiency rates with NAEP, the nation’s most reliable yardstick. If your state has set the bar lower, raise it, even though your numbers will look worse in the short run. Then set public goals for math and literacy in grades 4 and 8. Set goals for science and social studies, too. For more than a decade, these subjects have been squeezed down in elementary school schedules, and students’ knowledge has suffered, including the background knowledge that is essential to reading comprehension . Define, in measurable terms, what students should know and be able to do by the time they graduate from high school. And report progress publicly and in plain language, so parents know how their children are doing and communities know how their schools are doing. 2. Don’t just set goals. Help schools reach them. For years, the consensus was “tight on goals, loose on means”: set the targets and let schools figure out how to hit them. Experience has shown that most districts need more direction and more support. States won’t all take the same path, but every state owes its districts what it knows about what works. Here’s what your state education agency can do. Paint a clear picture of good instruction. Be clear about what “good” looks like and what you want to see in classrooms across your state. Articulate a vision in which every child is engaged in meaningful, relevant grade-level instruction every day . Ground this instruction in evidence about how children learn. And make sure every adult in the system — leaders, teachers, special educators, paraprofessionals and district staff — shares the same goal: to prepare and support every child to succeed in grade-level coursework. Put high-quality instructional materials in every teacher’s hands. A teacher’s job is to help students learn, not to write curricula and assessments from scratch. So equipping every teacher with strong materials is key. States have a critical role to play here. They can review materials for quality — what good materials look like differs by subject area and grade band — and encourage districts to choose strong ones. They can make sure the intervention materials used with struggling students actually prepare those students for their core classes . And they can offer research-informed guidance on when AI belongs in instructional materials, and when it doesn’t. Train teachers on the materials they actually use. Much ongoing professional development has little to do with what teachers teach every day. States can fund and support professional learning and coaching built around those materials , help districts choose strong providers, and align regional support centers with the state’s vision. Fix educator preparation. In many states, preparation programs for teachers and principals are disconnected from this vision of instruction . States already hold the levers to fix this misalignment (licensure, program approval and review) but rarely pull them. It’s time to start. Reward great teaching. States can encourage pay structures that reward teachers who get strong results with students, who lead their colleagues, or who take on the hardest assignments in the highest-need schools. Find out what is actually happening in classrooms. In too many states, “local control” has become a reason not to look. You can’t support improvement you can’t see. Gather information on the quality of instruction from districts, schools and classrooms, and use it to sharpen state policy and support. That commitment starts at the top. Before launching anything new, take stock of what your state is already doing. In some states, this work is well underway. Celebrate what’s working and build on it. Resist the urge to rethink existing work that’s sound. 3. Turn around struggling schools, for real this time States have spent two decades identifying and trying to improve low-performing schools, with too little to show for it. The states getting results set clear triggers for intervention, put proven strategies such as high-dosage tutoring in place and monitor closely enough to change course when something isn’t working. 4. Start early Last on this list but first in a child’s life: Make sure young children have access to high-quality childcare and early learning, so they arrive at kindergarten ready to learn. Invest in programs that build language and literacy, early math, social-emotional skills and healthy physical development. 5. Use the power of your office None of this happens without a governor’s sustained attention. Your state chief and education agency do the daily work, but only you can make student learning a statewide priority and keep it there. Four levers are yours alone. Appoint for capacity and continuity. Depending on your state, you appoint the state chief, members of the state board or both. Choose people who share this vision and know how to build a strong state agency, and ask them to stay long enough to see it through. The states that have improved held their strategy steady for years, across leaders and administrations. Make your first budget say what you value. Budgets are where priorities become real. Fund the work on this list: high-quality instructional materials, professional learning and coaching built around them, tutoring, early learning, and the state agency staff needed to support districts. Use new dollars to provide incentives for or require evidence-based uses rather than spreading those dollars thin. Legislate when necessary. Some of this work does need statute. But much of it depends on professional judgment and the freedom to adjust as you learn what works. Don’t lock that work into law. Give your education agency the authority and latitude to do it well, and hold it accountable for results. Use the bully pulpit, starting with your first State of the State. Tell your state the truth about how students are doing, name the goals you’ve set and come back to them every year. Visit the classrooms getting it right. Celebrate progress loudly and be honest when it stalls. When the governor keeps talking about student learning, everyone else in the system pays attention. Related Democratic Governors Must Prove Education Is a Priority. Here’s Where to Start None of this is theoretical. These lessons come from research and from the quiet work states across the country have done in recent years . For every recommendation above, there are states already doing it. There is no single right way to do this work. States have different laws, starting points and politics; their approaches need to work in their contexts. But we know this work can be done anywhere. We also know what happens when states abdicate their role in education: Some states are living with those results right now. Don’t let yours be one of them. Be an education governor.
authors: Joanne Weiss and Arne Duncan and Jack Markell

title: Unpacking Lessons Learned From Summit Learning, Part 2
summary: Class Disrupted is an education podcast featuring author Michael Horn and Futre’s Diane Tavenner in conversation with educators, school leaders, students and other members of school communities as they investigate the challenges facing the education system in the aftermath of the pandemic — and where we should go from here. Find every episode by bookmarking […]
content: Class Disrupted is an education podcast featuring author Michael Horn and Futre’s Diane Tavenner in conversation with educators, school leaders, students and other members of school communities as they investigate the challenges facing the education system in the aftermath of the pandemic — and where we should go from here. Find every episode by bookmarking our Class Disrupted page or subscribing on Apple Podcasts , Google Play or Spotify . Summit Learning — Summit Public Schools’ online platform created to help deliver and manage its blend of “personalized learning,” project-based learning and mentorship — attracted a lot of attention in the mid-2010s. And then it faded — fast. What lessons should the field learn from the last time an established and successful school network used a new technology and aimed to use it to both redesign itself and then offer that technology to other schools to help them transform as well? In the second of this two-part episode, Summit’s founder Diane Tavenner digs into the lessons learned from the platform she helped design, specifically diving into lessons learned about and for teachers, administrators, parents, students and technologists. Listen to the episode below. A full transcript follows. Diane Tavenner: It turns out they really, really care about their future, almost all of them. Michael Horn: Who knew? Diane Tavenner: They really care about their future. They’re thinking about it. They’re wondering about it. They don’t actually know what they’re doing in school and how it’s connected or related as a general rule. And so when Summit Learning comes in and it starts with like, what are your goals? Michael Horn: They probably don’t know how to answer that question up front. One, they tried to do— they did not go with a coalition of the willing, so they forced it on a grade level or a team or something, and they— or they didn’t give the students and the families opt-in choices. Michael Horn: OK. Diane Tavenner: They just said, You’re in, period. Yep. And so, that’s one big— and then, some of them were just bad communicators about that too. It’s just bad leadership and management, right? And then, the other piece was some of them didn’t implement the whole model, and when they would shortchange it, what they would do— so, mentoring was the hardest because it required— so, they would be like, oh, we can’t quite do that yet, but we’ll do it later, we promise. Can’t do that. Or, well, we can’t quite do the projects yet, so we’re only gonna do the content knowledge. And that became a— Michael Horn: We talked about the scores. Diane Tavenner: Yeah. And so basically they would take their normal English class, they would put kids on the playlist and, like, pretend that that was gonna be English. No, it’s not designed for that. That’s— well, and then no wonder people don’t like that. In those particular places, a couple of them where that was happening, there were some anti— quite frankly, anti-technology in schools, and then anti-Facebook people who had nothing to do with education but saw this as an opportunity, to go after that, and literally went in and organized and activated parents. And so we’ve referred over the years many times to this New York Times article, so it’s probably fair to just say what it actually was. The New York Times ends up writing an article called in by some of these, you know, advocates to this small town, introduced to this small, you know, handful of people. Diane Tavenner: And they write a front-page article on The New York Times about the major backlash to— Michael Horn: Quote-unquote major. Diane Tavenner: To this program, which is basically— and how Silicon Valley, Big Tech, Mark Zuckerberg is gonna try to come in, and it’s the classic stuff, steal your kids’ data and, like, force them on computers and all of this stuff. What’s crazy about that article, and this is why I didn’t read the New York Times for seven years, was one, riddled with just factual errors. So they had a picture on the front page of this family whose daughter has epilepsy, and they literally made the claim that Summit Learning was causing her to have seizures. That young woman was not in the Summit Learning program, had never used Summit Learning, had never been on the Summit Learning platform. Michael Horn: Really? Diane Tavenner: And the superintendent of the district actually, she says that, sends a letter to The New York Times, is like, this is factually inaccurate. You misreported it. Michael Horn: Nothing. Diane Tavenner: Their answer was, well, it’s Summit Learning-like. She uses things like Summit Learning. And what is that? Google. The internet. So, like, that’s how egregious it was. And then the second part was— I did not know this at the time, but The New York Times chooses which comments are posted. Michael Horn: Oh, for real? Diane Tavenner: For real. And they choose to not post comments. And so our community was trying to post responses to the article, and not a single one was ever allowed. Wow. Okay. So that was my disassociation with that publication. Michael Horn: Well, I was gonna say that also is a lesson about media and I guess distrust that’s been earned by it. Yeah. Diane Tavenner: But I think it’s so important in the moment we’re in because we’re seeing it. I mean, I feel like I’m watching this movie again. Michael Horn: The movie again. No, I’m glad we’re— Diane Tavenner: Which is, these anecdotes and these individuals really can drive policy for an entire school or system. Yeah. Michael Horn: Three points that I think you’ve made, but I just want to make very clear because they’re my takes as well. Number one, the opt-in, opt-out. It’s one of the biggest reasons I’ve moved to this choice posture as so important because I get it. There are some families that want the Waldorf-like nature-based school. I mean, we’ve seen from Tyler Thigpen, you can do nature-based and technology, but they don’t want any of that. And so they have made that choice and fine. Diane Tavenner: Yeah. Michael Horn: Great. Diane Tavenner: Great. Partial implementations of Summit model Michael Horn: But don’t screw it up for the family that’s going to get a benefit from it. So that’s number one is I think there’s, districts have such a one-size-fits-all mindset. And it is not— it doesn’t mean you’re building a school that you wouldn’t send your kid to, but, like, there are variations that are important to honor, I think. Diane Tavenner: And when we talk about the industrial core and mindset this whole year, that’s a huge part of the industrial mindset. One-size-fits-all. It’s an industry. It’s a factory, right? Michael Horn: Yeah. And I think it’s been one of the biggest reasons that in general, the response has been so paltry coming out of COVID is the inability to recognize that variation is real. Second, you mentioned the inability to communicate. I think that says something, and again, I don’t mean this in a derogatory way to the administrators, but they haven’t been taught about change management, communications. And it turns out, particularly in these public roles, that is a big part of your job. Diane Tavenner: Huge part. Michael Horn: And you’ve not been prepared for it probably in the previous roles you’ve come up through schools to get into that position. I was talking I was talking recently with a group that does stuff around technology in schools, and I was like, I would forget the technology part of your mission for the next couple years and just focus on communications and change management, because I don’t think you even have the right right now to think about, do we use this AI thing or not? Diane Tavenner: And to be fair to school leaders, and I mean, who, what leaders in our society are really winning on this right now? I mean, it’s a brutal environment to be leading in, period. Michael Horn: 100%. And then the third thing, just to say it in the quote-unquote implement— or I was going to say bad, but I’ll say partial implementations of Summit, where they said, forget about the mentoring, forget about the projects, we’re just going to do the 45 minutes of knowledge. Even the people who are big core knowledge adherents, they visited, as you know, some of these schools, and they hated it as well, because it didn’t really feel like engaging with knowledge. It felt like a bunch of clicking through stuff and very low level. And that was not— I’m a big believer in the importance of knowledge to learn, and this isn’t what they were talking about. And so without that integration in the model, a lot was being lost, I think. Diane Tavenner: It was. It was. Michael Horn: Last question on this. So those are my three points that I think just amplified what you said. But the data piece of it, that was a big piece of this narrative, was oh, Facebook’s taking your data. I’m not sure what people imagined that they would do with the data with kids, but, like, you have talked about how you could see data of kids spiking or flatlining and then spiking again and stuff. How should we think about the use of data and the collection of it in this moment and improvement? Diane Tavenner: Yeah. I mean, a couple of things. And I said I could see the data, we could see the data, because our team was literally partnering with educators, and we were partnering with researchers too. So it wasn’t that we weren’t doing research, we weren’t doing RCTs, but we did do some really cool research on it. Michael Horn: Yeah. Diane Tavenner: I just think that there is this tension between privacy and security of data. And to do a really good job in educating people as a teacher, as a parent, as the student yourself, you need good data. Michael Horn: Yeah. Diane Tavenner: And good data is game-changing. And so how do we think about that and get comfortable with that and be responsible with that? But again, it’s not this all or nothing where just ban the data. Michael Horn: Right. Diane Tavenner: And then the other thing I would say for this moment in time, because now it’s coming up around, you know, the hyperscalers or the big LLMs, the OpenAI, Anthropic, they’re taking your data, they’re training on your data. In my conversations with the folks in those companies, they literally say, no offense, but you all are worried about the wrong thing. The last thing we want to do is, like, take kids’ data and train on it. That is— that’s like a— that is like an offense that we don’t want to commit. Michael Horn: Because it’ll mess up our models. Diane Tavenner: It’s a brand. Michael Horn: Yeah. It’s not— and we don’t want to do that. Diane Tavenner: And it’s really been helpful for us. Yeah. Michael Horn: It’s helpful in a moment. Diane Tavenner: And so we are actively working so we don’t do that. Michael Horn: Interesting. Diane Tavenner: So there’s a lot of things you can be worried about, but that— like, you’re kind of focused on the wrong thing. Michael Horn: Interesting. Diane Tavenner: And so, and I mean, people have accused Bill Gates forever of this, which is just crazy to me. Like, Bill Gates is not looking at your kids’ data. I’m sure someone out there is now going to say that. I’m like, whatever. Michael Horn: Well, actually, let me make the point also though, because I was— so when I wrote Disrupting Class, I think there’s an unstated assumption in there that the software or online programs that we were sort of starting to profile were taking data from what was happening in classrooms with it and improving the product, ideally being able to start creating varied pathways and stuff like that. And I was horrified, to be honest with you, that none of that was happening when I actually got to talk to those executives. And there were a couple of reasons for it. All the data was generally trapped on the district side, and they had not created agreements that even allowed them to do it. Diane Tavenner: Yeah. Michael Horn: Forget about adaptive for a second. Like, Netflix was already learning from data at this point and being able to help present different pathways or movies you like. None of that was occurring in education. And so there was no, like— compared to the textbook— Diane Tavenner: The benefit of using the technology is lost. Michael Horn: Right. Compared to the textbook of using it to improve yourself. Compared to the textbook is, there was no feedback. Diane Tavenner: Right. Michael Horn: And we had just thrown out. And so now, like, it was almost like, well, of course it’s not that inspiring or interesting or improving because we’re all doing it based on anecdotes as opposed to really what happened. Diane Tavenner: Right. Michael Horn: And that was crazy to me. Diane Tavenner: So you’re losing the whole advantage of the education. Michael Horn: And I’m terrified in this AI moment with all this legislation that, like, I think in the effort to protect privacy, we will once again lose out on the benefits that could happen. Diane Tavenner: I know. I agree with you. Michael Horn: So, okay, let’s go macro, maybe sort of where do we leave this all? Worst question ever. But what are the, like, conclusions you are drawing? So we’re in this moment, we’ve just fast-forwarded into this. Like, what are the conclusions you’re drawing that sort of, you know, as people redesign— let’s talk high school specifically. Diane Tavenner: Yeah. Michael Horn: That people should hold in mind or need to be true as they do this work so they don’t repeat some of those mistakes or things that happened. Diane Tavenner: As we go there, could we talk a little bit, a minute about the technology? Because they’re, Michael Horn: Yeah. Diane Tavenner: Oh, yeah. Michael Horn: Sorry. Yeah, please. Diane Tavenner: Because there’s some really important learnings out of that. Michael Horn: Yeah. What did you learn about— and what did you learn about the people that built it? Diane Tavenner: Yeah. And I think it’s so relevant for this moment. Michael Horn: OK. Yeah. Diane Tavenner: So here’s what I learned, and this was a big eye-opener for me, and I, like, use this knowledge every day. So at the time, Facebook is attracting the world’s best engineers. Michael Horn: Right. Diane Tavenner: I mean, we literally had some of the world’s best engineers. Embarrassment of riches. We had this incredible team and designers and product people and whatnot. And I’d never built a technology product before. And so, like, I’m learning from them. So, here’s a couple of things I learned. One, there’s a huge difference between how you build a consumer-facing product and what people call a SaaS product or an enterprise product. Michael Horn: Enterprise, yeah. Diane Tavenner: And for most of us in education, well, we talk, like, we kind of treat technology like a black box. And I joke that, like, there’s the guy who’s kind of the part-time wrestling coach, Benji, who’s running around back there with cords and stuff, and we don’t know what he does, and we kind of don’t want to. Michael Horn: Yeah. Diane Tavenner: We just sort of want it to work. But we actually have to start educating ourselves as educators to be good partners with technologists because it’s a part, they don’t know anything about education. They don’t know how it works and what, and we’ve got to partner with them, but we’ve gotta actually know a little bit about what they do. Michael Horn: Well, so it’s interesting, right? ‘Cause like the consumer, we always say, is right, but if the consumer’s not asking the questions, how are they gonna, how are we gonna get what we need? Diane Tavenner: So when you think about the difference between a consumer-facing product and a SaaS product, and Facebook was a consumer product, right? And what we needed to build, I’ve now decided, that’s between the two. It’s like a hybrid version. Michael Horn: OK. Diane Tavenner: But we need to build a product that we have a full vision for because we actually have an outcome that we care about that we want for kids or multiple outcomes. Michael Horn: And it’s not just engagement. Diane Tavenner: In a consumer-based project, you’re just trying to like get them to use it and stay on there. And they are the actual decider, the consumer, the kid. But in our model, we actually have to meet the needs of teachers and administrators and parents. So it’s much more complex. Michael Horn: This is always my 5-level chessboard is like the jobs to be done of every single one of those has to line up. Yeah. Agile vs. Waterfall in Education Diane Tavenner: So it has to have significant parts of that enterprise model as well as the consumer model. And those teams build differently. They think differently. They build differently. They draw their, like on the consumer side, you’ll do a lot of like A/B testing over here on this side. No, you like make a blueprint and then you’re building towards it and you have a hypothesis. And so there, that’s a different build, number one. Number two, There’s these 2 ways of sort of building technology, waterfall or agile. And again, we want a hybrid here in education. Almost everyone builds agile now. And now with AI, I don’t even know what— yeah, that’s weird. But you need the hybrid because in waterfall, what you do is you literally plan out the entire thing you’re going to build. And I watch some school people doing this now. They will— go and contract with a company to build something. And that’s waterfall, where they like map the whole thing out that they’re going to build. And that means you can’t change things as you go. You’re not iterating on your learning. Agile is like, oh, I’m going to build this one piece first and then the next and learn and learn, which also doesn’t work as a school because you can’t start the school year with like, okay, I got this little piece and I don’t know when the next piece is showing up. And you’re like, well, in two weeks I need it. So what’s happening? So we need the hybrid. Michael Horn: So, some big cycle mismatch, I guess. Diane Tavenner: Exactly. And as I fundamentally believe in this moment, educators have to partner with technologists to be able to move us forward. And we’ve got to educate ourselves. And I want the technologists to understand this isn’t just another normal thing that they do. Michael Horn: And let’s just double-click again. The partnership is not just around building the product for my school as it exists. It’s the partnership is around the redesign, and I need your technology to help me redesign. So there’s like a very integrated way of operating to do this right at the moment. Diane Tavenner: Right. And one of the hard parts about technologists is they all went to school. Michael Horn: Right. Diane Tavenner: And so they build stuff for their experience in school. Michael Horn: As it has been. Diane Tavenner: As it has been. They’re not— they don’t know how to build for the school system we’re imagining as a general rule. Michael Horn: Gotcha. Okay, so now let’s flip to these macro conclusions that we can take away from as we pull into this moment. You’ve already hit a bunch of them. Diane Tavenner: Yeah. And so this is probably— I mean, for me, the big thing is we’ve got to think about this idea, and we’ve talked about this a lot. We talked about this with Reid last year, you know, innovation. We are not going to move away from the industrial school model, one teacher at a time, one classroom at a time. Like— Michael Horn: Right. And to be explicit, like, they’re still stuck in their model. So, like, it’s literally not going to— Diane Tavenner: They can’t. They can’t do it. And so we actually have to be conceptualizing, sort of elegant, aligned, integrated, whole-school models that bring all the stuff we know, all the pieces in a way that you can actually operate them. Michael Horn: Mm-hmm. Importance of supportive tech infrastructure Diane Tavenner: So that’s number one. And number two, it is impossible in this day and age to do that without a technological infrastructure that supports it. And the biggest thing that I saw from Summit Learning was because the technology was intentionally designed to support what we wanted to happen and what we cared about and what we valued, it reinforced the behavior. It helped with the change management. It made the data what we needed to see. It made it stick. And so, and we don’t have many, we, all of our tech is mostly industrial model, right? And so as we move forward, you gotta make this mindset switch and you gotta— Michael Horn: But it means building in partnership with what is, relatively speaking, a small number of schools that are ready to make that jump and redesign at the moment. And so— Diane Tavenner: Yes. But that’s my other learning is, I think sometimes people, when they talk about school models, they want, and we know lots of people who are like, we want hundreds or thousands of models. I don’t actually think there are hundreds or thousands of models. I literally think there’s a few. If you get these elegant, aligned, let’s even just get one. Can we just get one? And then when communities implement that by design, if it’s elegant and aligned and a precision model, it will have its own flavor. It will, when people go there, they will think, oh, this is its own thing, even though underneath it— Michael Horn: Yeah. I mean, I think my take has always been there’s certain principles that should scale. And then the bespoke way you customize it for this community, we’ll go back to the West Virginia versus Florida, our study of the natural environment around us will have slightly different content. Diane Tavenner: Yeah, right. Michael Horn: But the competency-based or mastery-based core, just to name one, should be consistent across those because it’s in line with what the evidence suggests around learning. Diane Tavenner: It’s the metaphor of the house, right? Like, what should be common and what is common in our current system? The foundation, the walls, the plumbing, the infrastructure. Like, that’s all common. It is pretty common even in every school in America today. It’s industrial, right? Michael Horn: Yeah. Diane Tavenner: And then how you— the chair you choose or the color background or your paint, that’s the stuff communities really want to personalize. Michael Horn: And great. Yeah. Okay. Super interesting. What is it going to take? I guess this goes back, and this is why I guess we ordered it the way we did, because we had this notion of the core, a new core into which these flavors of new models, model can fit. But I’m going to guess because you were doing this in districts that were stuck in the industrial core, there were a lot of incentives fighting back against these change efforts. Should we give a breath on what that’s going to take. Diane Tavenner: Well, we should because, and maybe this will help people understand sort of why my current point of view is we need to be building in partnership the new core for, I think I’m starting to call it this Precision Core, and the models, the actual schools themselves at the same time informing each other and building together because the Summit Learning Platform was an early version of a Precision core. Michael Horn: Right. Diane Tavenner: But it existed in states and districts that had these industrial pressures. So even though they would do this, then they would have to do these crazy backflips to, like, report to their state or translate, you know, the rubric into specific grades. Or, I mean, I remember— because you can imagine in 40 states, we were dealing with all these different policies, all these different requirements. And so often we would meet with teams, and initially they’d be like, oh, we can’t do that. And we’d say, why? We’d do the five whys. Well, why? Well, and when you got down to it, more often than not, there were not actual laws that were preventing it or even procedures. A lot of it was cultural. There were certainly some though, in terms of compliance and expectation that people were just having to plug back into that old system. And that just over time— Michael Horn: Drains energy. Diane Tavenner: You just can’t do it. Yeah. Michael Horn: Yeah, yeah. It’s interesting. My favorite example of this still that I think makes it real for people is when the virtual schools were born in 1999, 2001, somewhere around there. And they had to do back— here’s a model built for competency or mastery-based learning, and they had to do backflips to align it into seat time rules for kids who were learning all over the place. And then what resulted, out of that, I would argue a decade later, is virtual school models that were much more focused on seat time than learning. And then we acted surprised that the learning outcomes weren’t great. Diane Tavenner: Right, exactly. And that, that’s exactly what happens is like you get this burst of energy to sort of pull away from the industrial model and you do that for a little bit. And then over time, the gravitational pull back into it is just no one can resist that over time. Michael Horn: And I think these are the mutually reinforcing behaviors, processes, priorities at every level of the system. And I guess the way I sketched it out before we started talking about this was at one level you have your core, or what I would call a value network, which is all the actors plugging in with each other and how they connect and the rhythms. What do they exchange? What are their dependencies? Underneath that, you have the organizational or school or business models. Diane Tavenner: Mm-hmm. Michael Horn: And then you have strategy, I think, sits underneath that. Diane Tavenner: Interesting. Michael Horn: And then underneath that, you have your teams and your individuals and your culture. Diane Tavenner: OK. Michael Horn: And I always talk with my students, like, the reason we always say culture eats strategy for lunch is actually they’re connected. Like, on the day-to-day decisions you make, that’s your actual strategy. And vice versa, right? If you haven’t intentionally shaped that culture at the level of individual and team sitting inside a school, you’re sort of leaving culture to chance. Diane Tavenner: Which is why our commitment to the big summer experience and the ongoing was so important, and the embedding those values and that core into the technology. Michael Horn: And there’s a big piece of it I think you’d probably say is that probably starts with measuring outcomes pretty differently. Diane Tavenner: Completely. That’s the biggest thing. Michael Horn: Just double-click, yeah, finish this sentence. Diane Tavenner: Yeah, which is, again, and it was the critique and why people— but none of our schools came to us and said, we want to get 1.5 years of growth across all of our schools on average on a state test. That was not— that is not what’s driving humans around this. Instead, they were like, we don’t think we’re serving our kids, and we’re not sending them off into the world ready for the world. That’s what we want to do. But that’s not what our system measures or values. That’s imperative. And that goes at the heart of a lot of— Michael Horn: But that means measuring from the individual, not at the system level, and sort of a grassroots vision of that, which is more like the percentage of students served well relative to their goals, as opposed to, did I hit 1.5 years? Diane Tavenner: Yeah. People used to ask me, well, if you were going to— because I’d be so frustrated that I would get this like, end-of-year test result for my child, like, 4 months later, right? Michael Horn: Yeah. Parent concerns about child’s future Diane Tavenner: And I’m like, I’m in this. I do this every day. I can’t— what is this telling me? What does this mean? I don’t know what this means. And they’d be like, well, what do you want us to send that would have actual accountability? There’s no measures. I’m like, okay, I want you to send me the answer to 3 questions. One, does my child have a vision for where they want to go after high school? Yes or no. Do they have a vision and do you know what it is? Yes or no. Two, are they on a pathway that has a chance of leading them to that vision? Michael Horn: So it’s aligned. Diane Tavenner: Yes or no? Michael Horn: Yeah. Diane Tavenner: Three, are they making adequate progress on that pathway that I could credibly see them getting into that vision at the age of like, you know, 20? Just send me the answers to those 3 questions. Michael Horn: That’s a huge mindset shift. Diane Tavenner: But it’s the one we need. Michael Horn: Yeah. Diane Tavenner: And then I want to know at your school, how many of your kids have yes to all of those answers? And when they don’t, what are you doing about it? Michael Horn: Yeah. There’s two other things that I think are probably on your mind, which is who do you do this with initially and how do we fund it in a sustainable way to move toward that model? What are your final reflections on those two as we wrap up? Collaborative approach for technology building Diane Tavenner: So maybe my biggest takeaway is we did this as a single sort of school entity, and I can’t imagine trying to do that now, even with all the philanthropy. To me, this is just a coalition of people, and I think the more of us who think like this, want this, collaborate and come together, mostly because we need to collectively build the technology and the core. No one can do that by themselves. You’re not going to change it. You’ll be able to do your top model and then you’ll just get pulled back into it. Michael Horn: Sucked back in. Diane Tavenner: And so we’ve got to come back, come together as a coalition. And so that’s, as you know, that’s all I care about anymore is like, who can I collaborate with and work with on this? And then I think the second piece— Now I’m forgetting Michael Horn: Yeah. Financial. You got the financial. Diane Tavenner: Oh, the financial. How could I forget that? Michael Horn: Let me ask the question this way, because I think a lot of people are going to say you had an embarrassment Diane Tavenner: We did. Michael Horn: You had, you know, one of the wealthiest people in the world choosing to not just use his wealth, but the company to support you and build this. And what if we get that deal? I mean, there’s— you know this— there’s some big companies being formed right now. There’s a lot of wealth being formed right now. These opportunities could present themselves again. Diane Tavenner: Yes. Michael Horn: What’s your advice? Diane Tavenner: Well, I think that if I were to go back now, I thought I was doing a good job by getting philanthropy to commit for— to make it free to schools. Michael Horn: Yeah. Diane Tavenner: I actually do think there’s a huge role for philanthropy initially to do the initial builds and to sort of do that sort of risk capital upfront of like, we don’t know if this is gonna work, you know? Michael Horn: Yeah. Diane Tavenner: Build it, build it. But there does have to be a sustainable model. And it really does mean that like redoing the model of the school, we need to redo the financial— the financials of schools. I mean, I think you and I both believe money’s actually not the problem in education, and lots of people argue that. Michael Horn: Sure. Diane Tavenner: But there’s a lot of money. Michael Horn: There’s a lot of money, yeah. But it’s all tied up. Diane Tavenner: It’s all tied up. And I just am not willing to throw my hands up and be like, well, that’s how it is. Michael Horn: Yeah. Diane Tavenner: We gotta tackle that. Michael Horn: I think that’s probably a pretty good place to leave, I think, a very interesting set of conversations. I’m excited to hear people’s reactions to these lessons learned. For those of you not watching, Diane just made a face at that. Diane Tavenner: I’m excited. Michael Horn: If you’re watching— Diane Tavenner: Couldn’t tell. Michael Horn: Yeah, nervous-cited. But we’re excited to hear the feedback back. Diane Tavenner: Yeah. Michael Horn: Because I think with this fuller accounting, what we do with this in this moment is what’s so important. Diane Tavenner: Yeah. Michael Horn: And so I hope it helps people. Diane Tavenner: Me too. Michael Horn: I hope it helps the builders out there because we need people building this new core. Diane Tavenner: Yeah. Michael Horn: And we’ll take the feedback. I think we’ll skip the reading and other recommendations. And we just really want your take on what we have just offered and walked through. And Diane, let me say this, thanks for doing it with us. It puts you in a bit of a vulnerable position to revisit a lot of your professional career. I’m glad you let me ask the questions. Diane Tavenner: I appreciate the supportive space. And more, you know, what matters most to me is like literally taking the learnings and moving them forward. Yeah. Michael Horn: And there’s some checkered pieces of it that we’ve talked through. And so I think I appreciate the willingness and candor. Diane Tavenner: Yeah. Well, thank you. Michael Horn: Yeah. For all of you tuning in, we’ll see you next time on Class Disrupted. Disclosure: Diane Tavenner founded Summit Public Schools and served as its CEO from 2003 to 2023. This episode is sponsored by LearnerStudio.

Under pressure to do well on an exam, University of Virginia graduate student Kara Guyton was home taking a test last Thursday, joined by her three elementary school children, who made forts with blankets while students in other parts of the commonwealth were in class. In Albemarle County, Guyton’s kids and others were out of the classroom because school leaders discovered that over 500 employees had not undergone proper screening, forcing families to make daily arrangements for more than 14,000 children beginning last Thursday. Guyton said the closure announcement was “gut-wrenching” because she knew it would affect her family, with four school days before Thanksgiving. The closure could stretch past the break, depending on how long the employee screenings take. Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. The decision followed the school division’s review of employee Child Protective Services Central Registry screenings, which had never been submitted to the Virginia Department of Health, despite clearing initial criminal history checks. This follows a series of resignations and arrests involving school employees and leaders over the past six months. Three school board members also resigned amid claims of public mistrust and administrative collapse. Three school officials also faced misdemeanor counts for failure to report suspected child abuse. A view from outside the Albemarle County Office Building. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury) On Oct. 15, leaders of the Albemarle County Board of Supervisors formally requested accountability measures from the school board and assistance and oversight from the Virginia Department of Education, which said in an Oct. 27 memo obtained by the Mercury that “meaningful state action is now necessary.” The agency added it “remains committed to working collaboratively with the local school board and division leadership to navigate this crisis to ensure any gaps, deficiencies, and blind spots related to policies, protocols, and organizational culture are identified and addressed transparently so that student safety is prioritized, and trust is rebuilt with staff, families, and community members.” Soon afterward, Acting Schools Superintendent Chandra Hayes initiated internal review and uncovered the three-year administrative failure to submit 524 staff members for CPS Central Registry screening. Hayes confirmed that none of the individuals currently under active law enforcement investigation or criminally charged with abuse, neglect, or failure to report were part of the unsubmitted group. Legal and policy drivers Hayes cited two state laws and a board policy as the reasons she closed the schools beginning Thursday, saying employees must be vetted before students return. “Families should not have to accept any uncertainty about the adults working with their children, and I will not risk the safety of our students,” Hayes said in the announcement. The laws she raised focus on requiring schools to thoroughly check an applicant’s criminal and child abuse history before hiring them. Anyone with a confirmed history of child abuse, or certain criminal convictions, cannot be employed by the school. Hayes also referenced the school board’s policy calling for the immediate termination of a school employee if they are officially found responsible for child abuse or neglect and all appeals have been completed. The school division is required to terminate their employment and may recommend that the state revoke their teaching license. In the aftermath, Albemarle schools continued meal service at cafeterias last Thursday and Friday and offered asynchronous learning tasks to students. Child care before and after school was canceled. The superintendent said the division set a target reopening date of Nov. 30, after Thanksgiving, subject to confirmation by Friday. Guyton, like other parents who spoke with the Mercury, said she understands the need to close the schools completely, but the future is still concerning. “I think that my fear at this point is what’s next, and it seems like every month we are hearing about … a scandal, a personnel issue, or it’s our former principal getting arrested, and it just feels like this upheaval of this year is never ending,” Guyton said. About a quarter of the students come from economically disadvantaged families during the 2025-2026 school year, and nearly 14% have some disability. Christina Ra, a Family Council Officer for Albemarle County Schools, said ACPS serves a diverse range of families, so the division’s crisis plans should account for how closures affect different students and families — including access to food, childcare, transportation and school activities — rather than relying on each school to improvise. The Family Council hosted parents, some of whom were irritated by the division’s actions, along with ACPS Chief Communications Officer Jason Grant, on a call immediately following the announcement. The meeting was originally a monthly council meeting to discuss technology and AI use in classrooms. “The frustration came because it was as though a lot of the implementation was quick and not as thoughtful and inclusive as it should have been,” Ra said. “Some reps expressed concerns about children being alone at home and not actually having food.” Parents and supporters gather on Nov. 20, 2026, the second day of Albemarle County school closures, to raise awareness of issues facing the school division. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury) Elise Clerkin, a parent who has older children, said it was important for her to rally with other parents outside of the school division’s offices on Friday because she is “really fed up” with being let down by Albemarle Schools, and so are her friends, some of whom are teachers. “I have respect for the new superintendent who’s coming in and doing her best in a terrible situation, but I’m honestly pretty furious,” Clerkin said. “You want at the very least to feel safe sending your kids to school, and you want them to be able to thrive in the public school environment, and I feel like we’ve just been let down.” Ben Pearson-Nelson, president of the Virginia Parent Teacher Association, said the closure and allegations shocked families and raised fears about student safety, accountability, and trust in school leadership. “I have no doubt in my mind that every school board member in the commonwealth is keenly aware and getting questions about what happened and what it means,” Pearson-Nelson said. “I envision a … double-checking of what processes are already in place, what mechanisms schools are using, and then also what holes exist.” Ra said Hayes has done an “incredible job” to improve things. However, she said accountability for rebuilding public trust must extend to the school board, not rest solely on the acting superintendent. Ra called for the school board to demonstrate the same transparency, communication, visibility, and commitment to improvement that it expects from Hayes. “Why is it her job alone?” Ra said. “We want to see accountability from the school board.” A sign reading “Honk if you support us” stands upright during a gathering of parents raising awareness about issues facing Albemarle County Public Schools, Nov. 20, 2026. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury) What’s next Albemarle schools said no make-up instructional days will be required because of the surplus hours built into the state-approved division calendar. The Secretary and Department of Education implemented expedited Central Registry screenings, established oversight of an independent investigation into systemic and organizational failures, and reinforced the Oct. 27 directive to ensure continued state-level coordination with ACPS interim leadership. Gov. Abigail Spanberger said in a statement that the division’s prior leadership “failed” the children and families they served, and neglected to follow the background-check law, and uphold the trust of the commonwealth’s citizens. “My administration is committed to the education and safety of every child in Virginia, and we will use every available tool to rectify this failure and ensure accountability,” she said. As of Monday, all processed CPS Central Registry background check applications have been cleared , with 12 applications still awaiting processing.
